title: Myasthenia Gravis: Fatigable Weakness, Respiratory Risk, and Treatment Safety
bottomLine: Myasthenia gravis causes fluctuating fatigable weakness, often ocular/bulbar, from impaired neuromuscular transmission. Diagnose with the clinical pattern plus antibody/electrodiagnostic evidence, assess respiratory and swallowing function actively, and treat crisis as an airway/ICU emergency rather than simply increasing outpatient medication.
recognize: Ptosis/diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, neck/proximal weakness and worsening with repeated use are typical.
Sensation and pupils are generally preserved; respiratory weakness can progress without dramatic limb weakness.
differentiate: Lambert-Eaton often improves with activity and includes autonomic features; botulism may involve pupils/autonomic symptoms; motor-neuron disease usually lacks fatigability.
Cholinergic toxicity can mimic weakness but is accompanied by excess muscarinic features and requires different management.
assessment: Ask about chewing/swallowing fatigue, voice change, dyspnea/orthopnea, recent infection, surgery, medication changes and pregnancy.
Assess bulbar function and objective respiratory strength when crisis is possible rather than relying on oxygen saturation alone.
workup: Use acetylcholine-receptor/MuSK antibodies and electrodiagnostic testing according to neurology; assess thymic disease with appropriate imaging.
Pulmonary function/negative inspiratory force-style respiratory measures guide crisis risk in monitored care.
management: Use pyridostigmine for symptomatic control and immunotherapy according to disease severity/specialty plan; thymectomy is indicated in selected patients.
Myasthenic crisis requires ICU-level respiratory monitoring/support plus rapid immunomodulatory treatment and precipitant management.
medicationSafety: Several antibiotics, magnesium, sedatives and other drugs can worsen neuromuscular transmission; review medications before prescribing.
Do not abruptly escalate pyridostigmine in respiratory failure without distinguishing crisis physiology and securing airway support.
counselling: Teach medication timing around meals/activity and which new drugs should prompt a myasthenia safety check.
Pregnancy and delivery require coordinated neurology-obstetric planning.
followUp: Track ocular/bulbar/limb function, adverse effects and immunotherapy monitoring.
Escalate recurrent crisis, refractory disease or diagnostic uncertainty to neuromuscular specialty care.
examTrap: Using normal oxygen saturation to rule out impending myasthenic respiratory failure.
oneLinePearl: In myasthenia, ventilation can fail before the pulse oximeter looks alarming.

title: Bell Palsy: Isolated Peripheral Facial Weakness After Stroke Is Excluded
bottomLine: Bell palsy is an acute peripheral seventh-nerve palsy involving forehead and lower face after central and alternative causes are excluded. Early corticosteroid therapy and corneal protection matter; atypical, recurrent, bilateral or multi-cranial-nerve disease requires broader evaluation.
recognize: Unilateral weakness of forehead and lower face, incomplete eye closure, altered taste, hyperacusis or retroauricular discomfort may occur.
Most cases evolve over hours rather than as a chronic progressive facial neuropathy.
differentiate: Forehead-sparing facial weakness with other focal deficits suggests a central lesion/stroke pathway.
Ear vesicles/severe pain suggests Ramsay Hunt syndrome; Lyme disease, parotid disease and other neuropathies can mimic Bell palsy.
assessment: Perform a complete neurologic and ear examination, assess eye closure/corneal symptoms, Lyme exposure context, pregnancy and diabetes.
Ask about recurrent/bilateral symptoms or other cranial-nerve deficits.
workup: Routine imaging is not required for a classic isolated presentation; investigate atypical, recurrent, progressive or multi-cranial disease.
management: Start corticosteroid therapy promptly when appropriate and protect the cornea with lubrication/taping strategies.
Add antiviral therapy selectively when severe palsy/zoster features make benefit plausible.
Refer persistent atypical or incomplete recovery according to severity/timeline.
medicationSafety: Consider glucose effects of corticosteroids and pregnancy context.
Eye injury risk continues until reliable closure/blink returns even if facial movement begins improving.
counselling: Teach eye protection and expected recovery trajectory while explaining which changes require reassessment.
followUp: Reassess eye safety and facial recovery; refer prolonged or atypical cases.
examTrap: Calling every facial droop Bell palsy without testing the forehead and the rest of the neurologic exam.
oneLinePearl: Bell palsy is isolated peripheral CN VII weakness—anything more deserves another diagnosis.

title: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: Median Nerve Entrapment, Not Every Hand Numbness
bottomLine: Carpal tunnel syndrome is median-nerve compression at the wrist. Diagnose from a compatible sensory/motor distribution and provocative pattern, look for weakness/thenar atrophy or alternate root/neuropathy causes, and reserve electrodiagnostic testing for uncertain, severe or procedural-decision cases rather than every mild presentation.
recognize: Paresthesia/numbness in thumb-index-middle/radial ring fingers, nocturnal symptoms and relief by shaking the hand are common.
Thenar weakness/atrophy indicates more advanced motor involvement.
differentiate: C6/C7 radiculopathy includes neck/root features and may extend beyond a median distribution; ulnar neuropathy affects a different sensory territory.
Diffuse bilateral symptoms may reflect polyneuropathy rather than isolated CTS.
assessment: Map sensation, thumb abduction/opposition strength and thenar bulk; assess neck/reflexes and other nerve distributions when the pattern is not classic.
Review pregnancy, diabetes, thyroid disease, inflammatory disease and occupational/repetitive-load factors.
workup: Clinical diagnosis is often sufficient for typical mild disease; electrodiagnostic studies help confirm uncertain diagnoses and grade severe disease before surgery.
management: Use nighttime neutral wrist splinting and activity/ergonomic modification initially for many mild cases.
Corticosteroid injection can provide temporary relief in selected patients.
Refer for surgical decompression when persistent symptoms, objective weakness/atrophy or severe electrodiagnostic findings justify it.
medicationSafety: Avoid chronic opioid treatment for an entrapment neuropathy.
Pregnancy-related CTS often improves postpartum, so definitive procedures should be individualized to severity.
counselling: Teach wrist-neutral positioning and explain that persistent motor weakness is different from intermittent tingling.
followUp: Reassess strength/sensation and functional impairment after conservative treatment.
examTrap: Ordering cervical imaging or EMG automatically before confirming whether the symptom distribution is actually median nerve at the wrist.
oneLinePearl: Map the nerve distribution first; then decide whether the wrist is the lesion site.

title: Low Back Pain With Radiculopathy: Root Symptoms Without Missing Cauda Equina
bottomLine: Lumbar radiculopathy is radiating root-pattern pain with neurologic features, but most uncomplicated cases improve without urgent imaging. Imaging becomes urgent when cauda equina, infection, fracture, cancer or progressive major motor deficit is suspected; routine early MRI can identify incidental abnormalities that do not explain symptoms.
recognize: Dermatomal leg pain, paresthesia, root-specific weakness/reflex change and positive tension signs support radiculopathy.
Back pain alone without neurologic root features is not radiculopathy.
differentiate: Cauda equina causes urinary retention/incontinence, saddle anesthesia and severe/progressive deficits and is an emergency.
Hip disease, peripheral neuropathy and vascular claudication can mimic leg symptoms.
assessment: Assess motor power, reflexes, dermatomal sensation, gait, bowel/bladder function, saddle sensation and red flags for infection/cancer/fracture.
Ask about trauma, fever, IV drug use, immunosuppression, osteoporosis and malignancy.
workup: Avoid routine imaging in uncomplicated early radiculopathy without red flags.
MRI is indicated urgently for cauda-equina/major progressive deficit and selectively for persistent symptoms when surgery/injection planning is being considered.
management: Encourage activity as tolerated, use non-opioid analgesic strategies and address sleep/function.
Refer urgent red flags immediately; persistent disabling radiculopathy despite conservative therapy may warrant spine/specialty evaluation.
medicationSafety: Avoid routine prolonged opioids or sedative polypharmacy; NSAID risks depend on renal/GI/CV context.
Gabapentinoids have limited benefit for many radicular presentations and can add sedation/falls risk.
counselling: Explain that MRI findings are common in people without pain and should be interpreted with the neurologic pattern.
followUp: Reassess neurologic deficit and function if symptoms persist or worsen.
examTrap: Ordering immediate MRI for every episode of sciatica while missing new urinary retention and saddle anesthesia.
oneLinePearl: Most radiculopathy can wait; cauda equina cannot.

title: Cervical Radiculopathy: Root Pattern or Cord Disease?
bottomLine: Cervical radiculopathy produces neck/arm symptoms in a root distribution, but the priority is distinguishing it from cervical myelopathy. Hand clumsiness, gait imbalance, hyperreflexia, pathologic reflexes or bowel/bladder change imply cord disease and require urgent specialist imaging/evaluation.
recognize: Dermatomal arm pain/paresthesia with root-specific weakness/reflex change supports radiculopathy.
Symptoms may worsen with neck movement/compression and improve with certain positions.
differentiate: Median/ulnar entrapment is peripheral and lacks upper-motor-neuron signs; shoulder pathology can cause arm pain without a neurologic root pattern.
Myelopathy produces long-tract findings, gait change and hand dexterity problems rather than isolated single-root symptoms.
assessment: Map strength, reflexes, sensation, gait and hand dexterity; assess Hoffmann/Babinski/clonus when clinically appropriate.
Ask trauma, cancer, infection risk and bowel/bladder symptoms.
workup: Imaging is selective for persistent/progressive symptoms and urgent for myelopathy, major weakness, trauma, infection or malignancy concern.
EMG/NCS can help when peripheral entrapment versus radiculopathy remains unclear.
management: Use activity modification, appropriate analgesia and physiotherapy for uncomplicated disease.
Urgently refer myelopathy/progressive major deficit; persistent severe radiculopathy may need spine/specialty assessment.
medicationSafety: Avoid prolonged opioid/sedative therapy for uncomplicated radiculopathy.
Manipulation/traction should not be used casually when myelopathy/instability is suspected.
counselling: Teach signs of spinal-cord involvement that require urgent reassessment.
followUp: Reassess objective weakness/reflexes and function rather than pain score alone.
examTrap: Treating gait imbalance and hyperreflexia as a simple pinched nerve.
oneLinePearl: Radiculopathy is a root problem; myelopathy is a cord problem and changes urgency.

title: Dizziness and Vertigo: Timing, Triggers, and Central Red Flags
bottomLine: Do not diagnose dizziness from adjectives alone. Use timing, triggers and targeted eye/gait/neurologic examination to distinguish BPPV, vestibular neuritis, orthostasis/arrhythmia and posterior-circulation stroke; HINTS is only for the appropriate continuous acute vestibular syndrome and only when the examiner is trained.
recognize: BPPV causes brief position-triggered vertigo with characteristic positional nystagmus.
Vestibular neuritis causes continuous acute vertigo without hearing loss; central causes are more likely with focal findings, severe gait/truncal ataxia or central nystagmus patterns.
differentiate: Presyncope requires cardiovascular/orthostatic evaluation rather than a vestibular label.
New unilateral hearing loss plus acute vestibular symptoms changes the differential and can be time-sensitive.
assessment: Define onset/duration/triggers; assess nystagmus/eye movements, gait, cranial nerves, cerebellar function, hearing and orthostatic vitals when appropriate.
Review sedatives, antihypertensives, hypoglycemics and alcohol.
workup: Typical BPPV usually needs no imaging; perform positional testing when indicated.
Urgent stroke-capable assessment/imaging is required for central features or high-risk acute vestibular syndrome.
management: Treat BPPV with canalith repositioning, not prolonged vestibular suppressants.
Use short-term antiemetic/vestibular suppressants selectively for severe peripheral symptoms; central suspicion requires stroke pathway.
medicationSafety: Sedating vestibular suppressants increase falls and can delay compensation when used too long.
Do not attribute new dizziness to a medication until BP/rhythm/neurologic danger has been considered.
counselling: Teach falls precautions and why persistent/atypical symptoms require reassessment.
followUp: Reassess persistent symptoms rather than repeatedly prescribing suppressants.
examTrap: Calling all spinning dizziness BPPV without checking gait or neurologic findings.
oneLinePearl: Timing + triggers + exam beats the word 'dizzy'.

title: Neuroimaging: Choose the Test for the Question
bottomLine: Neuroimaging is selected by the clinical question and urgency. Noncontrast CT is fast for acute hemorrhage/major trauma questions; CTA evaluates vessels; MRI is more sensitive for many ischemic, inflammatory, tumor and posterior-fossa problems. Imaging is low-value when the clinical syndrome has no red flags and results will not change management.
recognize: Acute stroke, head trauma, thunderclap headache and focal deficit often require urgent imaging pathways.
Stable migraine, simple syncope with normal neurologic exam and established uncomplicated epilepsy often do not require routine repeat neuroimaging.
differentiate: CT and MRI answer different questions; a normal noncontrast CT does not exclude all ischemia, inflammation or posterior fossa disease.
CTA/MRA are vascular studies, not substitutes for all brain imaging.
assessment: Define onset/timing, focal findings, trauma, anticoagulation, pregnancy, renal function/contrast issues, implanted devices and the specific diagnosis being considered.
workup: Choose imaging to test a prioritized hypothesis and use validated stroke/headache/trauma pathways.
Avoid incidentalomas from indiscriminate imaging when pretest probability is low and no management change is expected.
management: Escalate time-critical findings immediately and ensure ownership of incidental but clinically important findings.
When imaging is unnecessary, document the clinical reasoning and return precautions rather than ordering it defensively.
medicationSafety: Contrast decisions require allergy/renal context but life-saving vascular imaging should not be delayed by low-value routine testing.
Sedation for MRI carries respiratory/falls/logistical risk and should not be treated as trivial.
counselling: Explain what the selected test can and cannot show and why more imaging is not automatically safer.
followUp: Close the loop on radiology recommendations and incidental findings that genuinely require action.
examTrap: Ordering MRI for simple syncope with a normal neurologic exam because it is the 'best' imaging test.
oneLinePearl: The best scan is the one that answers the urgent clinical question.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Neurology and Emergency Medicine recommendations
Canadian Stroke Best Practices imaging pathways

title: Neuromuscular Junction Disorders: Fatigability, Facilitation, and Autonomic Clues
bottomLine: Neuromuscular-junction disorders cause weakness without primary sensory loss. Pattern distinguishes myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton and botulism: fatigable ocular/bulbar weakness, facilitation/autonomic features, or descending cranial/autonomic paralysis. Respiratory/bulbar involvement changes disposition immediately.
recognize: MG commonly causes fatigable ocular/bulbar/proximal weakness.

Lambert-Eaton often causes proximal leg weakness, reduced reflexes that improve after activation and autonomic symptoms; botulism can cause cranial palsies, fixed/dilated pupils and descending paralysis.
differentiate: Peripheral neuropathy produces sensory loss; myopathy usually lacks ocular fatigability; motor-neuron disease has different UMN/LMN patterns.
assessment: Assess ocular/bulbar symptoms, proximal strength, reflexes before/after activation, pupils, autonomic symptoms, respiratory strength, cancer risk and food/wound/toxin exposure.
workup: Use syndrome-specific antibodies/electrodiagnostics and malignancy/toxin evaluation under neurology/public-health pathways.
Do not delay botulism antitoxin/public-health action for confirmatory testing when the syndrome is strong.
management: Treat the specific disorder: MG symptomatic/immunologic therapy; Lambert-Eaton management plus malignancy evaluation; suspected botulism requires urgent antitoxin/supportive/public-health management.
Provide respiratory support early when ventilation is threatened.
medicationSafety: Magnesium and several antibiotics can worsen neuromuscular transmission.
Sedatives/opioids can compound respiratory weakness and require heightened caution.
counselling: Teach medication-trigger precautions for diagnosed MG and urgent return for swallowing/breathing changes.
followUp: Neuromuscular specialty follow-up is required for chronic junction disease; botulism care includes public-health closure.
examTrap: Diagnosing sensory neuropathy when weakness fluctuates but sensation is normal and ocular/bulbar symptoms dominate.
oneLinePearl: Weakness without sensory loss plus fatigability or facilitation points to the neuromuscular junction.

title: Movement Disorders Beyond Parkinson Disease: Name the Movement Before the Disease
bottomLine: Movement-disorder evaluation starts by describing the movement—tremor, chorea, dystonia, tics, myoclonus, ataxia or stereotypy—before naming an etiology. Medication/toxin causes and functional movement disorders are common enough that a careful phenomenology and drug history prevent unnecessary imaging and wrong treatment.
recognize: Chorea is irregular flowing movement; dystonia is sustained/intermittent patterned posturing; myoclonus is shock-like jerking; tics are suppressible stereotyped movements/vocalizations with urge in many patients.
Tardive dyskinesia follows dopamine-receptor-blocking exposure and may persist after drug changes.
differentiate: Essential tremor and Parkinson tremor have different activation conditions; akathisia is inner restlessness rather than chorea.
Functional movement disorders can have internal inconsistency/distractibility but are real neurologic symptoms, not malingering.
assessment: Describe activation condition, distribution, rhythm, suppressibility, sensory tricks, distractibility and associated neurologic signs.
Review antipsychotics/metoclopramide, stimulants, antiseizure drugs, toxins, family history and psychiatric/systemic disease.
workup: Testing is phenotype-directed: selected labs, MRI, genetics or metabolic evaluation only when the pattern supports them.
Video documentation can help specialist evaluation when events are intermittent.
management: Remove/treat reversible drug/toxin causes when safe; use disorder-specific therapy and refer complex/refractory disease to movement-disorders neurology.
Functional movement disorder management uses clear diagnosis plus rehabilitation/psychological approaches rather than repeated negative testing.
medicationSafety: Do not treat tardive dyskinesia by simply increasing the offending dopamine blocker.
Dopamine-blocking drugs can worsen parkinsonism/dystonia and should be reviewed carefully before prescribing.
counselling: Use neutral descriptive language and explain that the movement phenotype guides testing.
When functional disease is diagnosed positively, communicate that symptoms are genuine and treatable.
followUp: Track function, medication exposure and phenotype evolution; reassess when new neurologic signs emerge.
examTrap: Calling every tremor Parkinson disease or every unusual movement psychiatric before describing the movement itself.
oneLinePearl: First name the movement; then name the disease.

title: Neurologic Manifestations of Systemic Disease: When the Brain Is the First Clue
bottomLine: Neurologic symptoms may be the presenting sign of metabolic, infectious, autoimmune, malignant, endocrine, hepatic/renal or medication disease. Localize the neurologic syndrome first, then look for systemic clues; do not attribute focal deficits or acute encephalopathy to a known chronic systemic diagnosis without excluding time-critical neurologic causes.
recognize: Hypoglycemia/electrolyte disturbance can cause seizures/encephalopathy; liver/renal failure can alter cognition; autoimmune/vasculitic disease can cause neuropathy, stroke or CNS inflammation.
Cancer can present with brain/spinal metastasis, paraneoplastic syndromes or treatment-related neuropathy.
differentiate: Diffuse metabolic encephalopathy differs from a focal stroke syndrome, although both can coexist.
Steroid/immunosuppressant therapy changes infection risk and can itself cause neuropsychiatric/metabolic complications.
assessment: Localize first: focal cortical, spinal, peripheral nerve, muscle/NMJ or diffuse encephalopathy.
Review systemic symptoms, medications/toxins, cancer/autoimmune/endocrine/renal/hepatic disease, infection risk and pregnancy.
workup: Use targeted glucose/electrolytes/renal/liver/thyroid/inflammatory/infectious/oncologic testing plus imaging or CSF according to localization and urgency.
Avoid broad untargeted panels when a clear focal emergency pathway is already indicated.
management: Treat life-threatening neurologic syndromes immediately while correcting the systemic cause.
Coordinate specialty care when autoimmune, paraneoplastic, metabolic or organ-failure disease requires disease-specific therapy.
medicationSafety: Renal/hepatic failure changes clearance of sedatives, opioids, gabapentinoids, ASMs and many other neurologic drugs.
Immunosuppressed patients can have serious CNS infection with muted fever/inflammation.
counselling: Explain that neurologic symptoms sometimes reflect systemic physiology and require both neurologic and medical evaluation.
followUp: Close the loop on the systemic diagnosis and neurologic recovery rather than treating symptoms indefinitely.
examTrap: Explaining focal weakness as 'uremia' or 'liver disease' before excluding stroke.
oneLinePearl: Systemic disease can cause neurologic symptoms—but focal emergencies still earn their own pathway.
